units.unit: Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units
tenants in subdivided flats are poor and have little bargaining power, so landlords can raise rents freely
living conditions are bad and rents per square foot are very high
stronger rules protect families from sudden eviction and rent jumps
main counter-argument is that landlords will leave the market
a cap plus security of tenure means a landlord cannot threaten a big rise or eviction, so the tenant is less stuck
need evidence on what happened to tenants when control was introduced
need the counter-view about landlords and supply
need a basic definition of subdivided units and how many there are
D1 gives the definition and the rent control debate
D2 should show actual rent and stock numbers to check whether tenants face high rents
D1p3 says the 2021 ordinance only capped increases inside a tenancy, not the starting rent, so tightening has a clear gap to fill
D2p1 says stock kept growing after the ordinance, supporting me against the landlords-will-leave worry
D2p2 says rent growth slowed but burden went from 31 to 34 percent, so existing control did not fix affordability
refined position: tightening should target the initial rent, not just increases
if initial-rent caps shrink supply, my refinement could hurt the people I want to help
the SDU is their only option while they wait for public housing
provisional answer: support a softer version, limits on rises at renewal plus longer tenure, rather than a hard initial cap
source must show what happens to unit numbers under a hard cap versus a softer limit
source must show whether landlords would really exit or just complain
source must show whether tenants in a place with a cap ended up better or worse off
only have Hong Kong numbers from one period, so need other evidence
D6 separates hard caps from softer limits
D5 shows what landlords claim they would do
D7 is a real case of a cap and what happened to tenants
D11 asks tenants directly and favours tenure security, which tests my softer version
D6p4 and D7p3 show a hard initial cap helps incumbents and shuts out newcomers, the same people I want to protect
D5p2 is a threat but D5p3 admits no margin data, so landlord exit is less certain than they say
D11p1 and D11p3 say tenants prefer tenure security, which fits my softer version
changed position: no hard initial cap, but tightening through tenure security and a light band on rents
D2p2 shows burden still rose, so rent rules alone are not enough
pick option 1, claim, evidence, objection, reply
because my view really changed during research and the supply objection is the strongest part
the burden figure D2p2 goes in the claim, as proof the existing control is too weak
want the reader to see my earlier hard-cap thought briefly, because the change shows why the evidence matters
ask whether the archive shows anything on whether the landlord exit threat is believable beyond D5
D6p1 gives a size (3 to 5 percent of stock per 10 percent rent cut), so exit is real but partial, not total collapse
the two parts of my claim connect: existing control too weak on tenure and burden, and rent rules alone cannot fix a long queue, so tightening must focus on tenure
the earlier hard-cap thought will be a step before the objection
reply: supply risk real for hard caps (D6p2), but 2021-style limit did not shrink stock (D2p1), so tenure security plus light band is safer (D11p3)
evidence order: need, weak current rule, objection, reply
D11p2 argues enforcement effort should go to fire and ventilation inspection instead of rents; should I admit tightening rents is not top priority
revised position: tighten through three-year tenure security and a light band on initial rents, not a hard cap
reasons: hard caps shut out newcomers (D6p4, D7p3), tenants prefer security (D11p1), current rule leaves burden rising (D2p2)
treat D11p2 as a limit on my claim
D2p1 point sits in the reply with one sentence saying it works because the ordinance is second-generation (D6p2)
tenure security is cheap to enforce compared with policing every rent, so it fits D11p2 better than a hard cap
will say rent rules are second best to inspections and housing queue shortening
D6p1 is stock loss, related to exit but not a direct count of owners leaving, so I will say 'stock contraction' not 'exit'
'cheap to enforce' is my own inference from D11p2, not in the passages, so I will word it as my reasoning
